sources.title: The Father Calls the Son God and Yahweh the Creator in Hebrews 1:8-12
sources.author: Exegetical Research Archive
sources.topic: Deity of Christ · Old Testament in the New

chunks.section_title: Hebrews 1:10-12 Applies Psalm 102:25-27 Directly to Jesus
chunks.text_content: One of the most decisive proofs of the Deity of Christ in the New Testament is Hebrews 1:8-12. After quoting Psalm 45:6-7 ('Your throne, O God, is forever and ever') as the Father's direct address to the Son, the author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 102:25-27: 'You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of Your hands; they will perish, but You remain... You are the same, and Your years will have no end.' In Psalm 102 (verses 1, 12, 21-22), the psalmist is speaking exclusively to Yahweh God of Israel. By applying this passage to the Son, Hebrews 1 identifies Jesus as Yahweh the immutable, uncreated Creator of heaven and earth.

sources.title: Does the Quran Affirm the Bible or Contradict It? Examining Surah 3:3, 5:46-48, and 10:94
sources.author: Comparative Theology Archive

chunks.section_title: The Quran Explicitly Confirms the Preservation and Authority of the Torah and Gospel (Injīl)
chunks.text_content: Textual comparison demonstrates that the Quran places its readers in an inescapable logical bind regarding the Bible. Throughout the Quran, the text claims to confirm the previous Scriptures—the Torah (Tawrāt) and the Gospel (Injīl)—that were actively in the hands of Jews and Christians in the 7th century (Surah 2:41, 2:89, 3:3, 5:43-48). In Surah 5:47, the Quran commands Christians ('the People of the Gospel') to judge by what Allah revealed in the Gospel. In Surah 10:94, Muhammad himself is instructed that if he is in doubt about what was revealed to him, he must ask those who have been reading the Scripture before him. Moreover, Surah 6:115 and Surah 18:27 declare that 'none can change the Words of Allah.'

chunks.section_title: Objection Claiming the Bible Was Textually Corrupted (Taḥrīf)
chunks.text_content: Critics object that the Quran only affirms the 'original' Torah given to Moses and the 'original' Injīl given to Jesus, arguing based on Surah 2:75-79 that Jews and Christians corrupted (taḥrīf) the text of the Bible before the 7th century.

chunks.section_title: Rebuttal: Why Textual Corruption (Taḥrīf al-Lafẓ) Contradicts Both Surah 5:47 and Manuscript History
chunks.text_content: Historical and textual evidence shows that the 'corrupted before the 7th century' claim contradicts both the Quran and manuscript history. First, one cannot command 7th-century Christians to judge by a book they no longer possess (Surah 5:47, 5:68), nor can one verify revelation against corrupted scriptures (Surah 10:94). Second, full New Testament manuscripts (such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus) date centuries before the 7th century (4th century AD), proving the Gospel in the 7th century is the exact same New Testament read today—which teaches that Jesus is the divine Son of God who died and rose again. Therefore: if the Bible is true, any text that contradicts it cannot be true; and if the Bible were corrupted, any text affirming its 7th-century preservation would still be undermined.

sources.title: If Jesus Is God, Why Does He Pray to the Father? Incarnation, Trinitarian Communion, and John 14:28
sources.author: Exegetical Research Archive
sources.topic: Incarnation · Trinity · Prayer of Jesus & John 14:28

chunks.section_title: Why the Incarnate Son Prays to the Father (Philippians 2:6-8 & Hebrews 5:7)
chunks.text_content: When critics ask, 'If Jesus is God, why does He pray? Does God pray to God?', they confuse Unitarian modalism (the idea that the Father and the Son are a single person) with historic Trinitarian theology and the Incarnation. In biblical Christianity, the one eternal Being of God exists as three distinct, co-eternal Persons: the Father, the Son (Word), and the Holy Spirit (John 1:1; Matthew 28:19). Furthermore, in the Incarnation, the eternal Son genuinely assumed a complete human nature (John 1:14; Philippians 2:6-8: 'taking the form of a servant'). As a true, sinless man and our High Priest (Hebrews 5:7), Jesus prayed to His Father both to model perfect human dependence on God and to express the eternal interpersonal communion of love between the Son and the Father (John 17:1-5).

chunks.section_title: Objection: Does Jesus Praying and Saying 'The Father Is Greater Than I' (John 14:28) Prove Subordination?
chunks.text_content: Critics object: 'Prayer is an act of worship from an inferior creature to a superior Creator. Moreover, in John 14:28 Jesus explicitly says, "The Father is greater than I," and in Mark 13:32 He says only the Father knows the hour. Therefore Jesus is ontologically subordinate to God and cannot be co-equal with the Father.'

chunks.section_title: Exegetical Rebuttal on Functional Submission vs. Ontological Equality (John 14:28, Mark 13:32, John 17:5)
chunks.text_content: Classical Christian exegesis refutes this objection by distinguishing ontological nature (what someone IS) from positional/functional role (what office someone assumes). In John 14:28, Jesus explains WHY the Father is 'greater' (meizōn, greater in position/glory, not beltiōn, better in nature): 'because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.' While Jesus walked the earth in the humble state of a servant facing crucifixion, the Father reigned in unvarnished heavenly glory. That is why in John 17:5—inside His very prayer!—Jesus asks the Father to restore Him to 'the glory that I had with You before the world existed.' A mere creature never shared pre-cosmic divine glory with YHWH (Isaiah 42:8). Likewise, in His voluntary kenosis (Philippians 2:7), the Son refrained from exercising certain divine prerogatives according to His human nature (Mark 13:32) and experienced physical death in His humanity (1 Peter 3:18; Hebrews 2:9, 14) while remaining the eternal Lord of glory who raises Himself from the dead (John 2:19-21; 10:17-18).

sources.title: Does John 17:3 Disprove the Deity of Christ? Examining 'The Only True God'
sources.author: Exegetical Research Archive

chunks.section_title: The Objection from John 17:3 ('You, the Only True God')
chunks.text_content: Critics of the Trinity frequently cite John 17:3, where Jesus prays to the Father: 'And this is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.' They argue that since the Father is called the 'only true God' in distinction from Jesus Christ, Jesus is excluded from being the true God.

chunks.section_title: Contextual and Grammatical Refutation (John 17:1-5 & 1 John 5:20)
chunks.text_content: Contextual exegesis reveals three fatal flaws in this reading of John 17:3. First, by the exact same logic, since Jude 1:4 calls Jesus 'our only Master and Lord (monon Despotēn kai Kyrion)', one would have to exclude the Father from being Master and Lord! In biblical idiom, calling the Father 'the only true God' contrasts Him with false pagan idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), not with His own eternal Word and Son. Second, in John 17:3 itself, eternal life requires knowing BOTH the Father AND Jesus Christ equally. Third, just two verses later in John 17:5, Jesus asks the Father to glorify Him 'in Your own presence with the glory that I had with You before the world existed'—a pre-cosmic divine glory that Yahweh in Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11 never shares with a mere creature.

sources.title: Why Do You Call Me Good? Jesus' Question to the Rich Young Ruler in Mark 10:17-18
sources.author: Exegetical Research Archive

chunks.section_title: The Skeptical Claim on Mark 10:18
chunks.text_content: In Mark 10:17-18, when a man addresses Jesus as 'Good Teacher', Jesus replies: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.' Critics claim Jesus is rebuking the man and denying His own deity by contrasting Himself with God.

chunks.section_title: Socratic Analysis of Mark 10:17-22
chunks.text_content: Textual analysis notes that Jesus never says, 'I am not good, do not call me good.' Rather, He asks a diagnostic question: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.' In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus repeatedly claims prerogatives belonging exclusively to God—forgiving sins (Mark 2:5-12, where the scribes ask 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?'), being Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), and demanding absolute allegiance above family and possessions (Mark 10:21). By stating that God alone is intrinsically good, Jesus invites the ruler to connect the dots: if Jesus is truly 'Good', then He is not merely a human teacher, and following Him requires forsaking the man's idol of wealth (Mark 10:21-22).

sources.title: Jesus Christ as the Sovereign Lord (Kyrios) and Yahweh in Paul's Christology (Philippians 2:6-11)
sources.author: Exegetical Research Archive

chunks.section_title: Paul's Application of Isaiah 45:23 to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11
chunks.text_content: In Philippians 2:6-11, the Apostle Paul does not merely ascribe a high angelic or prophetic status to the Lord Jesus. By quoting Isaiah 45:23—a passage in which Yahweh emphatically swears by Himself that 'there is no other God besides Me' and that 'to Me every knee shall bow and every tongue confess'—Paul identifies Jesus within the unique sovereign identity of Yahweh Himself. The ‘name above every name’ bestowed upon the incarnate, risen Christ in Philippians 2:9-11 is Kyrios (Lord), the Greek Septuagint rendering of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH).

chunks.section_title: Common Objection on 'God Exalted Him'
chunks.text_content: Opponents object: 'If Philippians 2:9 says God highly exalted Jesus and gave Him the name above every name as a reward for His obedience, then Jesus could not have been God Almighty from eternity, because Almighty God cannot be exalted or given something He did not already possess.'

chunks.section_title: Rebuttal: Pre-Incarnate Glory vs. Incarnate Exaltation
chunks.text_content: Exegetical analysis shows that this objection ignores the flow of Philippians 2:6-8 and parallel texts like John 17:5. Verse 6 explicitly establishes that prior to becoming flesh, Christ eternally existed 'in the form of God' (en morphē theou) and possessed equality with God. Because He humbled Himself by assuming a true human nature ('taking the form of a servant'), His subsequent exaltation in verses 9-11 is the enthronement of the God-Man in His resurrected humanity to the very glory He shared with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5).

sources.title: The Quranic View of the Christian Trinity: Examining Surah 5:73, 5:116, and 4:171
sources.author: Comparative Theology Archive

chunks.section_title: Surah 5:116 and the Misrepresentation of Historic Trinitarian Theology
chunks.text_content: In Surah 5:116, Allah asks Jesus whether he told mankind: 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah (ilāhayni min dūni Allāhi).' Historical theology highlights that biblical Christianity has never taught tritheism (three separate gods) nor has it ever included Mary as a goddess in the Godhead. Rather, Christians believe in one eternal Being of God (Deuteronomy 6:4; Matthew 28:19) existing eternally as Father, Word/Son, and Holy Spirit. Consequently, the critique in Surah 5:116 and Surah 5:73 ('Allah is the third of three') addresses a triad misconception rather than the actual New Testament doctrine of the Triune God.

sources.title: Jesus as the Word of God (Logos / Kalimatullah) and Spirit from God in Comparative Perspective
sources.author: Comparative Theology Archive
sources.topic: Comparative Christology · John 1:1, Surah 4:171 & Sahih al-Bukhari 3448

chunks.section_title: Comparing Surah 3:45, Surah 4:171, and Sahih al-Bukhari 3448 with John 1:1-14
chunks.text_content: Both the New Testament (John 1:1, 1:14; Revelation 19:13) and the Quran (Surah 3:39, Surah 3:45, Surah 4:171) alongside Sahih al-Bukhari 3448 uniquely call Jesus the 'Word of God' (Logos / Kalimatullah) and 'a Spirit from Him' (wa-Rūḥun minhu), while Sahih Muslim 2365 and Surah 19:19 affirm his sinless purity. In classical Sunni theology, Allah's Word (Kalām) and Spirit are eternal uncreated attributes, yet commentators confronting Surah 4:171 and Sahih al-Bukhari 3448 often attempt to reduce 'Word' to merely the creative command 'Be!' (Kun).

chunks.section_title: Competing Explanation of 'Kalimatullah' as 'Kun' (Be!)
chunks.text_content: Commentators (citing Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Surah 3:59) argue that Jesus is only called 'a Word from Allah' because he was created without a human father by Allah's spoken command 'Be!' (Kun), just as Adam was created from dust by the command 'Be!'

chunks.section_title: Counter-Analysis of Surah 3:45, 4:171, and Sahih al-Bukhari 3448
chunks.text_content: Grammatical analysis shows why the 'Kun' reduction fails on the texts' own terms: First, everything in creation comes into existence by 'Kun', yet neither Adam nor any other prophet is ever personally named 'the Word of Allah' (Kalimatuhu) or 'a Spirit from Him' (Rūḥun minhu) as Jesus is in Surah 4:171 and Sahih al-Bukhari 3448. Second, in Surah 3:45 the grammar identifies the Word personally as the Messiah ('a Word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary'). In John 1:1-14, the rationale is explicit: Jesus is the eternal Logos who was with the Father in the beginning, through whom all things were created, and who entered human history in the Incarnation.

scriptures.text_content: Who, though he was in the form of God (en morphē theou), did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant... Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Kyrios), to the glory of God the Father.
scriptures.original_language_note: Greek: 'en morphē theou' (in the essential nature/form of God) and 'morphēn doulou labōn' (taking the form of a servant) — explains both why the Incarnate Son prays to the Father as a true servant and why every knee bows to Him as YHWH (Isaiah 45:23).

scriptures.text_content: There is no other god besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Hebrew: YHWH swears by Himself that every knee will bow to Him alone. Paul applies this unmistakable YHWH-text to the risen Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11.

scriptures.text_content: You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin).
scriptures.original_language_note: Greek: 'meizōn' (greater in position/glory) vs 'beltiōn' (better in nature). Jesus speaks from His state of earthly humiliation and incarnate servanthood before returning to the Father's heavenly glory (cf. John 17:5; Hebrews 2:9).

scriptures.text_content: In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word was with God (pros ton Theon), and the Word was God (kai Theos ēn ho Logos). He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made... And the Word became flesh (sarx egeneto) and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
scriptures.original_language_note: Greek: 'pros ton Theon' distinguishes the personal identity of the Logos from the Father, while the qualitative predicate nominative 'Theos ēn ho Logos' (Colwell's construction) identifies the Logos as fully divine by nature.

scriptures.text_content: But of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God (ho Theos), is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.' ... And, 'You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain... But you are the same, and your years will have no end.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Applies Psalm 45:6-7 and Psalm 102:25-27 (a prayer addressed directly to YHWH the uncreated Creator) directly to the Son by the Father Himself.

scriptures.text_content: And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do. And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.
scriptures.original_language_note: Greek: 'para seautō' and 'pro tou ton kosmon einai' — in His high-priestly prayer, Jesus claims pre-cosmic, eternal divine glory alongside the Father before creation.

scriptures.text_content: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Greek: 'ei mē heis ho Theos' — Jesus does not deny being good (in John 10:11 He calls Himself the Good Shepherd, 'ho poimēn ho kalos'); rather, He challenges the rich ruler to recognize the implication of his own title.

scriptures.text_content: And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, the son of Mary, confirming that which came before him in the Torah; and We gave him the Gospel (al-Injīl), in which was guidance and light and confirming that which preceded it of the Torah... And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein (wa-l-yaḥkum ahlu l-injīli bimā anzala Allāhu fīhi).
scriptures.original_language_note: Arabic: Commands 7th-century Christians ('People of the Gospel') to judge by the Gospel in their possession, creating a foundational textual dilemma when compared with New Testament Christology.

scriptures.text_content: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word (Kalimatuhu) which He directed to Mary and a spirit from Him (wa Rūḥun minhu). So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, 'Three'; desist - it is better for you.
scriptures.original_language_note: Arabic: 'Kalimatuhu' (His Word) and 'Rūḥun minhu' (a Spirit from Him). Uniquely in the Quran, Jesus is personally titled both the Word of Allah and a Spirit proceeding from Him.

scriptures.text_content: [And mention] when the angels said, 'O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him (bi-Kalimatin minhu), whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].'
scriptures.original_language_note: Arabic: 'bi-Kalimatin minhu' (a Word from Him), 'wajīhan fī al-dunyā wa-al-ākhirah' (illustrious in this world and the next).

scriptures.text_content: And [beware the Day] when Allah will say, 'O Jesus, Son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?"' He will say, 'Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Arabic: 'ittakhidhūnī wa-ummiya ilāhayni min dūni Allāhi' (take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah) — addresses a triad of Allah, Jesus, and Mary rather than the historic Christian Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

scriptures.text_content: Narrated 'Ubada: The Prophet said, 'If anyone testifies that None has the right to be worshipped but Allah Alone Who has no partners, and that Muhammad is His Slave and His Apostle, and that Jesus is Allah's Slave and His Apostle and His Word (Kalimatuhu) which He bestowed on Mary and a Spirit created from Him (wa Rūḥun minhu), and that Paradise is true, and Hell is true, Allah will admit him into Paradise with the deeds which he had done even if those deeds were few.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Authentic (Sahih) Hadith affirming Surah 4:171's unique titles for Jesus as 'Kalimatuhu' (His Word) and 'Rūḥun minhu' (a Spirit from Him), often examined alongside Tafsir Ibn Kathir.

scriptures.text_content: Abu Huraira reported Allah's Messenger as saying: 'No child is born but he is pricked by the Satan and he begins to weep because of the pricking of the Satan, except the son of Mary and his mother.'
scriptures.original_language_note: Authentic (Sahih) Hadith confirming the sinless preservation of Jesus (cf. Surah 19:19, 'zakiyyan' — a pure/faultless son) in contrast to all other human prophets.

source.title: Jesus' Claim to be the Eternal 'I AM' in John 8:58 and Exodus 3:14
source.author: Exegetical Research Archive

chunks.section_title: John 8:58 ('Before Abraham Was, I Am') and the Septuagint of Exodus 3:14 & Isaiah 43:10
chunks.text_content: In John 8:58, Jesus declares to His opponents, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was born, I am (prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi).' Grammatical analysis demonstrates that Jesus does not merely say 'I existed before Abraham' (which would require the imperfect 'ēmēn' as in John 1:1); instead, He uses the present-tense absolute 'egō eimi', echoing Yahweh's self-designation in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10-13 ('before day was, I am He'). That is why the audience immediately picked up stones to stone Him for blasphemy (John 8:59; cf. John 10:30-33).

chunks.section_title: Objection That 'Ego Eimi' Only Means 'I Am He (the Beggar)' in John 9:9
chunks.text_content: Critics point to John 9:9 (where the healed blind man says 'egō eimi') to argue that the phrase in John 8:58 merely means 'I am the one' rather than the divine name of Exodus 3:14.

chunks.section_title: Rebuttal on the Syntactical Contrast in John 8:58
chunks.text_content: Context and syntax govern meaning: in John 9:9 the blind man is simply identifying himself as the beggar, whereas in John 8:58 Jesus contrasts Abraham's coming into existence ('genesthai', aorist infinitive of 'ginomai') with His own timeless, eternal existence ('egō eimi', present indicative). Combined with John 8:24 and John 13:19, this directly echoes Yahweh's self-disclosure in Isaiah 43:10.
